claims.text: High-throughput combinatorial processing can create a continuous composition gradient in HfNbTaTiZr for determining individual constituent effects.
Increasing the Hf content of HfNbTaTiZr will increase hardness and yield strength relative to the equimolar alloy.
An equimolar HfNbTaTiZr alloy can provide a baseline with characterized microstructure and mechanical properties.
Additive manufacturing or combinatorial sputtering can produce HfNbTaTiZr samples with a controlled Hf composition gradient.
Nanoindentation and mini-tensile testing can rapidly map local mechanical properties across the proposed composition gradient.
Mechanical testing of compositionally complex alloys can be conducted from room temperature to elevated temperatures.
Precise process control can maintain phase stability across the Hf composition gradient.
Changing Hf content will cause localized grain refinement, altered lattice distortion, or altered dislocation pinning in HfNbTaTiZr.
Grain refinement in HfNbTaTiZr can be associated with high hardness.
Increasing Hf content enhances lattice distortion and atomic-size mismatch in HfNbTaTiZr.
The additional lattice distortion and mismatch impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion increases alloy hardness and strength.
Higher-Hf locations will show a systematic increase in hardness and possibly yield strength.
The expected increase in mechanical properties is approximately 10–20% relative to the equimolar baseline.
The predicted strengthening depends on the alloy remaining a stable solid solution.
Excessive compositional deviation may produce brittle intermetallic phases or phase separation.
The magnitude of strengthening will depend on microstructural evolution, processing parameters, and secondary-phase formation.
X-ray diffraction or electron microscopy can determine whether phase stability is maintained across the gradient.
Failure to observe a systematic mechanical-property increase with Hf content would falsify the directional prediction.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as conventionally processed, while the falsification experiment requires the equimolar baseline to be processed under conditions identical to the additively manufactured or sputtered gradient samples. These are not necessarily identical processing histories.
